notes.headline: Cisco: fastest growth in 15 years, yet the shares fell 5% — next quarter’s guide is below this one
notes.takeaway: Revenue rose 24% to a record $18.5 billion and adjusted EPS of $1.40 beat the $1.33 consensus, with AI infrastructure orders from the largest cloud companies now expected to reach $9 billion this year. But guidance for next quarter of $18.0–18.2 billion implies revenue falling from this quarter’s level, and the stock dropped 5.1%.
results: Cisco reported revenue of $18.5 billion for the quarter ended October 24, up 24% from $14.9 billion. Adjusted earnings per share were $1.40, up 40% and ahead of a consensus of about $1.33; reported EPS was $1.14, up 58%. The company called these its strongest revenue and adjusted EPS growth rates in more than 15 years.

The adjusted operating margin was a record 37.8%, and the reported margin was 30.2%. Adjusted net income was $5.6 billion against $4.0 billion a year earlier. Cisco said demand was broad, with double-digit growth across every geography and customer market.
The company declared a quarterly dividend of $0.42 per share. Revenue, adjusted operating margin and adjusted EPS all came in above the top of the ranges Cisco had guided to.
mgmt: Chief executive Chuck Robbins said the company is in ‘the very early stages of a multi-year networking supercycle’ as organisations rebuild their networks for AI workloads, and that Cisco is confident of capturing what he called a multi-billion-dollar opportunity.

Chief financial officer Mark Patterson said the business is unlocking significant operating leverage as it scales, which lets earnings grow much faster than revenue. Cisco raised its expectation for AI infrastructure revenue from hyperscale cloud customers to $9 billion for fiscal 2027, more than double the total for fiscal 2026.

For the second quarter Cisco expects revenue of $18.0 billion to $18.2 billion and adjusted EPS of $1.34 to $1.36. For the full fiscal year it raised guidance to revenue of $74.8 billion to $75.8 billion and adjusted EPS of $5.47 to $5.53.
view: For a decade Cisco was the definition of a mature technology company: low single-digit growth, a generous dividend and a share count shrinking through buybacks. Revenue growth of 24% and earnings growth of 40% are numbers this company has not produced since before the financial crisis, and they come from a real change. AI data centres need far more networking per dollar of computing than traditional ones, and Cisco — after years of being dismissed as a loser in the cloud — is selling into them. The $9 billion hyperscaler target is larger than many networking companies’ entire revenue.

So why did the shares fall 5%? Read the guidance against the quarter just reported. Cisco delivered $18.5 billion and is guiding to $18.0 to $18.2 billion next quarter — a sequential decline of 2% to 3%. Adjusted EPS is guided to $1.34 to $1.36 after $1.40. For a stock that had risen sharply on the idea of a supercycle, a guide that points down from here, even slightly, raises the question of whether this quarter contained orders pulled forward. The full-year range of $74.8 to $75.8 billion implies the remaining three quarters average about $18.9 billion, so the year as a whole still grows — but the path is flatter than the word ‘supercycle’ suggests.

The quality of the earnings deserves credit. A 37.8% adjusted operating margin on hardware-heavy revenue is exceptional, and it reflects both scale and the software and subscription revenue Cisco has built, partly through the Splunk acquisition. Earnings growing nearly twice as fast as revenue is what operating leverage looks like. The gap between adjusted EPS of $1.40 and reported EPS of $1.14 — amortisation of acquired intangibles and share-based pay — is wide, though, and worth keeping in view.

The risk is concentration of a new kind. Cisco’s traditional business was spread across hundreds of thousands of enterprises and governments, which made it dull and dependable. The new growth comes from a handful of hyperscalers whose spending is lumpy and who design much of their own equipment. A company can be both a beneficiary of the AI build-out and more cyclical than it used to be. At a valuation that has re-rated from a utility-like multiple to a growth one, the market now expects the supercycle; this quarter’s guide was the first reminder that the path will not be a straight line.
notes.watch: Second-quarter revenue against the $18.0–18.2 billion guide, and product orders. A beat that takes revenue above this quarter’s $18.5 billion would settle the pull-forward question; a result inside the range would leave it open.
